pmf> 
>>> version
version
build 460 date 20261030 time 073641
PureMetal Forge - Anvil, the Raspberry Pi 4 monitor. Version 2.0,
64-bit AArch64, running with no operating system underneath it.
  This is build 460 of this board's monitor, made 2026-10-30 at 07:36:41.
  The number is raised by one by every successful build, so two images
  can be told apart from the prompt. It says WHICH build this is, not
  WHAT is in it - a number can be reset, frozen, or carried by a source
  somebody edited without rebuilding. The digest below is what is in it.
  This monitor's own image is 6666700 bytes, 00200000 .. 0085B9CB.
  That extent is the RUNNING IMAGE's own: the compiler marks the end
  of the image with a symbol and this program reads it, so the length
  is of the code that is executing and not of a file on a disk that
  may since have been replaced. It is also why this monitor has no
  maximum size - type map.
  That size and the build number above are enough to tell two images
  apart. For the digest that says WHAT is in it, type:
    version full        - or crc32 00200000 0065B9CC
  It is not done here unasked because it reads every byte of the
  image, which is not instant on a board with its caches off.
  Built by PureMetal Forge for target pi4.
  This image is a kernel8.img. The firmware loads the whole file to
  00200000 and enters it there, with no loader in between -
  which is why its size is not capped by anything: there is nothing
  above it in the boot path to make room for.
  The compiler and linker versions are not stamped into the image, so -
  unlike U-Boot's version - they are not printed here rather than
  guessed at.
  Type info for the board, revision and clocks, or help for the commands.
pmf> 
>>> map
map
THE MEMORY MAP, AS THIS IMAGE MEASURES IT
  this image      00200000 to 0085B9CB   6666700 bytes, measured from the image itself
  reserved        00200000 to 008FFFFF   this monitor's code, measured from the image
  reserved        0D000000 to 0F6FFFFF   its variables, placed by --bss-addr
  reserved        001FF000 to 001FFFFF   the autoboot record
  reserved        08A00000 to 091FFFFF   the DSI framebuffer
  reserved        001FC000 to 001FEFFF   the reserved raw-secondary stacks
  reserved        09200000 to 099FFFFF   the driver-module arena and its staging window
  reserved        001FB000 to 001FBFFF   the boot phase record
  reserved        0B000000 to 0BBFFFFF   the screenshot capture area
  reserved        10000000 to 13FFFFFF   the reserved Vulkan device-memory heap
  its stack top   00100000               and it grows downwards from there
  stage a file at 00900000               which is what the upload tools ask for

Where a payload may go:
  the low window   00900000 to 07EFFFFF   (about 118 MB)
  the high window  40000000 to FBFFFFFF   (about 3 GB)
  Nothing in this map is a constant this program was told. The
  monitor's extent is the size of the image the firmware loaded, and
  the low window begins above it, so both move when this program
  does. There is no maximum size.
ok
pmf> 
>>> shot status
shot status
A capture on the next payload return is not armed.
  shot arm      arms it for the next run, once
  shot disarm   puts it back
  boot mem <address> shot   arms it and boots in one line
The capture area holds picture number 69, 1280 by 800 as the
console saw it, taken by this monitor as a payload returned (its x0 was 0000000000000000)
from 4096000 bytes of the 800 by 1280 surface the panel was scanning, at 90 degrees.
  shot          streams it, in the same format p streams the live screen
pmf> 
>>> net recv 5001 1000000
net recv 5001 1000000
Listening on port 5001 on every usable addressed interface for ONE connection:
    the Wi-Fi radio at 192.168.1.114
  Everything it sends goes to 01000000 and the last byte it may
  write is 07EFFFFF, which is 116391936 bytes.
  Send the file and close the connection; the length and the SHA-256 of
  what actually landed are printed here when you do. Any key stops it.
Received 150704 bytes from 192.168.1.104 to 01000000 in 79 ms.
  That is 1860 KB/s.
  sha256 9f62450bc470822c20d2857f6cc21320edae9a792c0514997cee84dd9596e4df
  The digest is of THE MEMORY, taken after the transfer, and it took 85
  ms. Compare it with sha256sum of the file on the host: equal means
  the bytes in this board's DRAM are the bytes in that file.
  THE DIGEST TOOK LONGER THAN THE TRANSFER, and that is instruction
  fetch rather than the hashing: on a board whose caches are off, every
  instruction of the inner loop is read from DRAM. If this board has a
  runtime cache switch, turning it on before the next upload is worth
  a factor of about sixty here. Type help to see whether it has one.
  Nothing has been booted and nothing has been written to the medium.
  boot mem 01000000 enters it if it is a container; save <name>
  01000000 00024CB0 writes it to the boot medium.
pmf> 
>>> deadman 15
deadman 15
The deadman watchdog is armed for 15 seconds.
  It covers the NEXT payload only. It is armed immediately before the
  jump and stopped immediately after, and it is never running while you
  are sitting at this prompt - a board that reset itself while somebody
  was reading a dump would be a rescue costing more than the thing it
  rescued from.
pmf> 
>>> last run
last run
LASTRUN 00000178 02 00 0F 0000000000000000 0000000001000000 00000000000004B9 0000000000000000 0000000000000000 0000000000000000
Run 376 entered the payload at 01000000 with a 15 s deadman armed.
It RETURNED after 1.2 s, and its x0 register held 0000000000000000.
  A host that did not see the return line lost it on the way; the
  payload itself came back.
pmf> 
>>> boot mem 1000000 shot
boot mem 1000000 shot
The frame this payload leaves on the screen will be kept before
anything repaints over it. Read it back afterwards with shot.
Placing 150576 bytes at 01000000, the address the payload was built for
  (from the container at 01000000).
Verifying 150576 bytes at 01000000 against the container's SHA-256 ...
  computed 4286ec306dd8a2783c5b0d60502ea3158491591cd41be34e0a416c4afe0594b4
  the digest matches the one the compiler put in the container.
Clearing 171616 bytes of zero-init memory at 01080000.
This payload was built to return to the monitor, so the prompt should
come back when it is finished.
This payload asked for the service table, so it is entered with x0 = 0EF62DF8
  (ABI 1.12, 200 slots). It can call back into this monitor.
Starting the payload at 01000000. Control leaves the monitor now, and
anything printed below this line came from the payload, not from Anvil.
The deadman watchdog is armed for 15 seconds. If the payload hangs and
never comes back, the board will reset itself rather than sit there.

It NEVER CAME BACK and the board restarted underneath it with the
  deadman armed, so THE DEADMAN RESET THE BOARD: the payload stopped
